question.text: What is the 'risk reversal' in options trading?

answer.text: Buying an OTM call and selling an OTM put (bullish) or buying an OTM put and selling an OTM call (bearish) — it creates a directional position with reduced or zero net premium
Reversing a previously opened option position
Converting a call option into a put option through an exchange mechanism
A regulatory mechanism to reverse trades found to be in error

explanation.text: The Logic: A risk reversal is a directional options strategy built from two OTM options on the same underlying with the same expiry. A bullish risk reversal buys an OTM call and sells an OTM put — the premium received from the short put helps fund the long call, so the trader gets upside exposure at reduced (sometimes zero) net cost, while taking on downside risk through the short put. A bearish risk reversal flips the structure: long an OTM put, short an OTM call. The Trap: "Risk reversal" is a specific strategy, not the act of unwinding an existing trade. It is not a mechanism for converting calls into puts inside the exchange, and it is not a regulatory error-correction tool — it is a voluntary trading strategy. Note: The NISM Series I (Currency Derivatives) and Series VIII (Equity Derivatives) workbook pages reviewed cover option spreads, vertical spreads (bullish/bearish), and single-leg currency option speculation, but the specific term "risk reversal" and the long-OTM-call/short-OTM-put structure were not located in the workbook pages reviewed. The framing above is presented as general options-strategy industry knowledge rather than a workbook citation.
